title: Check for Listening – Communicating Confidence
author: Wood, Nick
summary: Nick Wood describes a finger-based confidence-check technique he layered onto a Sparx Maths "Insights"-driven Do Now routine with his Year 8 class: after students answer a retrieval question individually, he asks them to show 1 to 5 fingers indicating how confident they are in their answer, before deciding whether to cold-call a student to explain or to model the solution himself. He is careful to caveat the account with context, including a higher-prior-attainment group and his position as interim deputy head teaching only this one class, while still reporting that the technique noticeably increased both visible engagement and the class's willingness to participate compared to before. He walks through the full routine in detail: projecting a question, silent individual work, the "Show me" confidence signal, deciding whether to model or hand over to a student based on the aggregate confidence shown, then repeating with a paired question to check whether confidence has genuinely risen. Wood frames the post primarily as a way of thinking through his own practice in public, inviting scrutiny of whether the technique would transfer to less confident or less motivated classes and to his fuller timetable next year.
points: Wood's core mechanism is using aggregate visible confidence, not correctness, as the decision point for whether to hand a question to a student or model it himself, making the confidence signal do real instructional work.
He explicitly separates "checking for listening" from "checking for correctness": the technique surfaces engagement and self-assessed understanding even before he checks whether answers are right.
His repeated-question design, asking, signalling confidence, addressing gaps, then asking a paired question and re-signalling, is built to make a change in confidence visible within the same lesson.
He is unusually explicit about the limits of his own evidence, one higher-attaining class and one teacher, which sharpens rather than undermines the account's credibility.
quotes: All caveats aside, what I can say is that I noticed a change in the class response to me when I started doing this, and that the benefits that Pritesh describes in terms of the number of hands up as a proxy for engagement were visible using this technique from the moment I started to employ it.
I say, “When I say ‘Show me’, I want you to raise your hand showing how confident you are in your answer to this question: 1 finger is not at all confident, 5 fingers is very confident.
At this point, pupils raise their hands, and I get a quick scan. I can now see if there are pupils who are not engaged.

Every time I use this method, the class report of confidence is higher. Again it is decision time – if we are at all 4’s and 5’s now, I use turn and talk to get pupils to share with partners, then ask if any pairs had different answers.

This method of checking for listening by confidence has become a staple part, not just of the ‘Do Now’, but for other parts of lessons, and supports building a culture where pupils engagement in the task at hand is normalised.
